title: Official talk
job: Announcements, offices and counters: the formal register you hear
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Arabic makes a passive by changing the VOWELS INSIDE the verb, not by adding an auxiliary: kataba becomes kutiba, yaktub becomes yuktab, dafaʿa becomes dufiʿa. Because this course writes every short vowel, the passive is visible on the page.

The Arabic passive CANNOT NAME ITS AGENT. There is no by-phrase: yumnaʿ at-tadkhīn min al-mudīr is not a sentence. If who did it matters, the sentence must go back to the active. That is a rule, not a style note.

Every passive cell is a separate surface from its active one and gets its own row here, pointing back at the verb's first-teach row — the same way L3-M4 handled its jussive cells, and for the same reason: a level never edits a file below it.
yurjā, it is requested, in front of a maṣdar is the polite public announcement: yurjā al-intiẓār. It takes a noun, never a verb, and it is aimed at everybody and nobody.
yumnaʿ, it is forbidden, is the prohibition a guard speaks. It stands BESIDE L3-M8's participle mamnūʿ rather than replacing it: the sign reads mamnūʿ at-tadkhīn and the guard says yumnaʿ at-tadkhīn.
THE PLURAL OF POLITENESS: min faḍlikum, tafaḍḍalū and the plural imperative are what a clerk uses to ONE person. The number is deference, not arithmetic, and English has nothing that does this.

English officialese is passive AND wordy. Arabic officialese is passive and NOMINAL: it prefers a maṣdar where English prefers a clause — at the moment of boarding, not when you board. That is L3-M1's maṣdar doing its third job.

English politeness at a counter is interrogative — could you possibly, would you mind. Arabic politeness is impersonal: yurjā, yajibu ʿalayka. A British question translated straight into Arabic sounds evasive rather than polite.
You have already met one of these without knowing it was a system: L3-M10's wulidtu and wulida, I was born, he was born. That u-i shape is the passive, and this module is where it becomes a pattern.

sentences.display: yurjā al-intiẓār fī aṭ-ṭābūr ḥattā yaʾtī ad-dawr
sentences.script: يرجى الانتظار في الطابور حتى يأتي الدور
sentences.cue: Please wait in the queue until your turn comes
sentences.literal: It-is-requested the-waiting in the-queue until he-comes the-turn

words.note: The announcement verb, and a passive: nobody is doing the requesting. It takes a noun behind it, never a verb.
The maṣdar of L2-M10's intaẓartu — the waiting, as a thing. This is the noun yurjā is built to take.
The queue at a counter. The article assimilates to the ṭ, so it is written aṭ-ṭ- and heard as one long ṭ.
Your turn in a queue. ad-dawr ʿalayka, the turn is on you, is what a clerk says to call you forward.

sentences.trap: The English is an imperative aimed at you — please wait. The Arabic names no one at all: it is requested, and the request hangs in the air over the whole hall.
sentences.sound: yur-JĀ: the j is the soft one of French jour in much of the Levant and the hard English j in Egypt; either is heard here.

variations.cue: Please wait here
variations.changed: the shortest form of the announcement, with no clause at all

variations.cue: Booking is requested before arrival
variations.changed: a different maṣdar behind yurjā, and L3-M1's al-wuṣūl behind qabla

mistake.display: hal mumkin an tantaẓir fī aṭ-ṭābūr?
mistake.script: هل ممكن أن تنتظر في الطابور؟
mistake.why: A British counter question. Politeness in Arabic officialese is impersonal, not interrogative — a question here sounds evasive rather than polite, as if the clerk were unsure of the rule.

sentences.usage: What a loudspeaker or a sign at a counter says to everybody at once.
sentences.mnemonic: yurjā asks nobody and everybody: a verb with no doer, then a noun.

sentences.cue: Smoking is forbidden in the office

words.note: The guard's prohibition, and yurjā's opposite number. It stands beside L3-M8's mamnūʿ rather than replacing it: the sign reads mamnūʿ, the guard says yumnaʿ.

sentences.trap: English can name the forbidder — smoking is forbidden BY MANAGEMENT. Arabic cannot: there is no by-phrase behind a passive, and adding min plus a person turns the sentence into nonsense.
sentences.sound: yum-naʿ: the final ʿayn is a squeeze low in the throat that stops the word; it is not the hamza catch of yabdaʾ.

variations.cue: Smoking forbidden in the office
variations.changed: L3-M8's participle in place of the verb — what the sign shows rather than what the guard says

variations.cue: Smoking is forbidden here
variations.changed: the place, cut to one word

mistake.why: A by-phrase. The English passive can name its agent and the Arabic passive cannot — min al-mudīr reads as forbidden FROM the manager, which is not a sentence anybody says.

sentences.usage: A sign, a guard, or a recorded announcement setting a rule.
sentences.mnemonic: mamnūʿ is painted on the wall; yumnaʿ comes out of a mouth.

sentences.cue: The name was written on the form

words.note: The passive past. Arabic makes a passive by changing the VOWELS inside the verb: kataba, he wrote, becomes kutiba, it was written.
The passive present of the same verb, and the same trick one tense on: yaktub becomes yuktab.
The name. On an official form it is what goes in the first box.

sentences.trap: English builds a passive out of two words — WAS WRITTEN — so a learner looks for an auxiliary to add. Arabic adds nothing: the letters are the same and only the vowels move.
sentences.sound: KU-ti-ba, against KA-ta-ba: three syllables either way, and the u in the first is the whole message.

variations.cue: The name was written here
variations.changed: the place, and nothing else

variations.cue: The name is written on the form
variations.changed: the present of the same passive — a standing rule rather than a finished act

mistake.why: The ACTIVE vowels with a passive meaning. kataba says the name did the writing; because this course writes every short vowel, the error is visible on the page.

sentences.usage: Reading back what an official form already contains.
sentences.mnemonic: Same letters, different vowels: kataba does it, kutiba has it done.

sentences.cue: The fees are paid at the window

words.note: The passive of L3-M8's tadfaʿ, one vowel apart from it. A non-human plural takes the feminine singular verb, so rusūm takes tudfaʿ.
The fees or charges an office takes. It is a plural and behaves as a feminine singular for the verb.
The hatch you queue at. The article assimilates to the sh, so it is written ash-sh- and heard as one long sh.

sentences.trap: English can say WHO pays — the fees are paid by the passenger. Arabic will not: if the payer matters, the sentence has to go back to the active tadfaʿ.
sentences.sound: TUD-faʿ: the u after the t is the passive; tadfaʿ, with an a, is the ordinary you-pay of L3-M8.

variations.cue: The booking is paid for at the window
variations.changed: a masculine singular subject, so the passive takes the y- prefix

variations.cue: The fees are paid here
variations.changed: the place, cut to one word

mistake.why: L3-M8's active vowels. tadfaʿ says the fees pay something; the a and the u are the only things carrying the difference.

sentences.usage: The standing rule a counter announces about money.

sentences.cue: The office will be closed in an hour

words.note: L1-M6's sa- written joined in front of a passive present. The particle costs nothing extra: only the verb's vowels are doing the passive work.

sentences.trap: English needs three words for this — will be closed — and a learner assembles them one at a time. Arabic needs one written word, and the whole passive is inside its vowels.
sentences.sound: sa-YUGH-laq: the gh is the gargled r of French, and the sa- in front is unstressed.

variations.cue: The office closes in an hour
variations.changed: without sa- — a standing fact rather than an announcement about today

variations.cue: The window will be closed in an hour
variations.changed: what closes: the office becomes the counter hatch

mistake.why: The active vowels: yughliq means he closes something, so the office is doing the closing. Only the i for the a tells the two apart, which is why this course writes them.

sentences.usage: The last announcement before a public office shuts.
sentences.mnemonic: sa- says when; the vowels say who is not doing it.

sentences.cue: The office is opened every day

words.note: The passive of open, and yughlaq's opposite. Its past is futiḥa, with the same u-i vowels as kutiba and dufiʿa, and its future sa-yuftaḥ.

sentences.trap: English opens is both transitive and intransitive — the office opens at eight — so no passive feels needed. Arabic makes the choice explicit and the office does not open itself.
sentences.sound: YUF-taḥ: the final ḥ is the breathy throat h, not the light h of hunā.

variations.cue: The window is opened every day
variations.changed: what opens

variations.cue: The office is open every day
variations.changed: L3-M8's participle, which reports a STATE where the passive verb reports an event

mistake.why: The active vowels again. yaftaḥ makes the office the opener; the passive u-a pattern is what says somebody opens it.

sentences.usage: Opening hours, as an office states them.
sentences.mnemonic: maftūḥ is how it stands; yuftaḥ is what is done to it.

sentences.display: yuʿlan ʿan taʾkhīr al-qiṭār fī al-maḥaṭṭa
sentences.script: يعلن عن تأخير القطار في المحطة
sentences.cue: The train's delay is announced at the station
sentences.literal: Is-announced about delay the-train in the-station

words.note: The loudspeaker's verb, passive like the rest. It reaches its topic through L4-M2's ʿan: announced ABOUT the delay.
A delay, as a noun. The hamza sits on the alif in the middle and is written ʾ, never ʿ.
The noun of the same root: the announcement itself, whether spoken or posted on a board.

sentences.trap: English says the station announced the delay and puts the doer first. Arabic officialese removes the doer entirely, which is why a translated version of the English sentence sounds like an accusation.
sentences.sound: yuʿ-LAN: the ʿayn closes the first syllable, so the word starts with a small squeeze before the l.

variations.display: yuʿlan ʿan taʾkhīr al-ḥāfila fī al-maḥaṭṭa
variations.script: يعلن عن تأخير الحافلة في المحطة
variations.cue: The bus's delay is announced at the station
variations.changed: what is delayed

variations.cue: The notice was written at the station
variations.changed: the noun instead of the verb, under S03's passive past

mistake.why: The station named as the announcer. It is grammatical Arabic but it is not the register: an official announcement has no agent, and naming one moves the sentence into news reporting.

sentences.usage: What comes over a platform loudspeaker.

sentences.display: yajibu ʿalayka an tadfaʿ ar-rusūm al-yawm
sentences.script: يجب عليك أن تدفع الرسوم اليوم
sentences.cue: You must pay the fees today
sentences.literal: It-is-necessary on-you that you-pay the-fees today

words.note: L3-M2's yajibu with the duty laid on a person: the frame stays in the he-form and ʿalā carries the pronoun.

sentences.trap: English puts the person first — YOU must pay. Arabic puts the obligation first and hangs the person off a preposition, so the sentence opens with a verb that agrees with nobody.
sentences.sound: ya-JI-bu ʿa-LAY-ka: yajibu keeps its final -u because it is a frozen frame, and the stress falls on the -lay- of ʿalayka.

variations.display: yajibu ʿalayki an tadfaʿ ar-rusūm al-yawm
variations.script: يجب عليك أن تدفع الرسوم اليوم
variations.cue: You must pay the fees today (to a woman)
variations.changed: the pronoun on ʿalā, which is where the addressee lives

variations.display: yajibu ʿalayka an tadfaʿ ar-rusūm qabla al-ḥajz
variations.script: يجب عليك أن تدفع الرسوم قبل الحجز
variations.cue: You must pay the fees before the booking
variations.changed: when — L3-M1's qabla with a plain noun behind it

mistake.why: A free pronoun where ʿalā belongs. yajibu never takes a subject; the person is only ever a pronoun stuck to ʿalā.

sentences.usage: A clerk telling you what the rule requires of you.
sentences.mnemonic: The duty comes first, and you arrive on top of ʿalā.

sentences.cue: Please, come this way to the window

words.note: The plural of politeness. A clerk says it to ONE person: the -kum is deference, not a count of how many are standing there.
The plural of L2-M5's tafaḍḍal, used the same way — one customer, plural verb, because the register raises the number.

sentences.trap: English marks counter politeness with softening words — if you could just — and keeps the number honest. Arabic marks it by moving one person into the plural, which an English speaker hears as a mistake.
sentences.sound: min faḍ-LI-kum ta-faḍ-ḍa-LŪ: the doubled ḍ in tafaḍḍalū is held, and the -ū at the end is long.

variations.cue: Please, come this way to the office
variations.changed: where you are being sent

variations.cue: This way please, kindly wait here
variations.changed: the invitation followed by the announcement — the two registers in one breath

mistake.why: Half plural and half singular. Once the register lifts the addressee into the plural, every word aimed at them goes with it.

sentences.usage: A clerk or an usher moving somebody along politely.
sentences.mnemonic: One customer, plural words: the number is the politeness.

sentences.display: ḥaḍratuka, hal maʿaka al-huwiyya wa al-ḥajz?
sentences.cue: Sir, do you have the ID and the booking?
sentences.literal: Your-honour, question with-you the-identity and the-booking?

words.note: Your presence — the polite you a clerk uses instead of anta. It is a noun with a pronoun on it, so it changes for a woman: ḥaḍratuki.
The ID card an office asks for. The word is identity itself, used for the card that carries it.
A booking — of a seat, a room or an appointment. It is the thing yurjā asks for in S01's second variation.

sentences.trap: English politeness at a counter goes into the verb — could I see, would you mind. Arabic leaves the question plain and lifts the PRONOUN instead, which has no English equivalent at all.
sentences.sound: ḥaḍ-RA-tu-ka: the ḥ is the deep breathy one and the ḍ is heavy, so the first two syllables sit low in the mouth.

variations.display: ḥaḍratuki, hal maʿaki al-huwiyya wa al-ḥajz?
variations.cue: Madam, do you have the ID and the booking?
variations.changed: the whole line addressed to a woman

variations.cue: Sir, kindly wait in the queue
variations.changed: the polite address in front of S01's announcement

mistake.display: anta, hal maʿaka al-huwiyya wa al-ḥajz?
mistake.why: The bare anta at a counter. It is not rude in itself, but it drops the register the whole exchange is conducted in, and next to ḥaḍratuka it lands as brusque.

sentences.usage: The first thing a clerk says to you at a window.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥaḍratuka is you with a hat on.
